1 --- 2 title: Designing view transitions 3 description: Learn how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation, loading, and content changes in a Next.js app. 4 nav_title: View transitions 5 --- 6 7 In web apps, route changes replace the entire page at once. Morphs, reveals, and crossfades carry less risk since they affect smaller areas or rely on opacity rather than position. 369 370 The simplest approach is to disable all animation durations: 371 372 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 373 @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { 374 ::view-transition-old(*), 375 ::view-transition-new(*), 376 ::view-transition-group(*) { 377 animation-duration: 0s !important; 378 animation-delay: 0s !important; 379 } 380 } 381 ``` 382 383 Without animation, content swaps instantly, which is the browser's default behavior. A more refined approach would preserve crossfades and opacity transitions while removing positional movement. See ["No Motion Isn't Always prefers-reduced-motion"](https://css-tricks.com/nuking-motion-with-prefers-reduced-motion/) for more on this. 384 385 ### Step 4: Crossfade content within the same route 386 387 The gallery has a photographer section with tabs. Each tab shows a different photographer's photos, but the route structure is the same: `/collection/[slug]`. Clicking between tabs does not feel like navigating to a new page. It feels like switching content within the same container. 388 389 A directional slide would be wrong here. Slides communicate "going to a new place." A crossfade communicates "same place, different content." The container persists (continuity), only the grid inside changes (swap). 390 391 Use a `ViewTransition` with `key` set to the current slug. When the key changes, React triggers a transition between the old and new content: 392 393 ```tsx filename="app/collection/[slug]/page.tsx" 394 import { Suspense, ViewTransition } from 'react' 395 396 export default async function CollectionPage({ params }) { 397 const { slug } = await params 398 399 return ( 400 }> 401 408 409 410 411 ) 412 } 413 ``` 414 415 The `share="auto"` and `enter="auto"` props tell React to use its default crossfade animation. The `name` prop gives the container an identity so React knows what to animate. The navigation triggers the transition; the `key={slug}` change makes React treat the old and new content as an exit/enter pair (activating `share`) instead of an in-place update. 416 417 If we click between photographer tabs, the grid crossfades. The tab bar and surrounding layout do not move. Only the photo grid transitions between states. 418 419 ## Next steps 420 421 You now know how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation. Shared elements communicate continuity across routes. Suspense reveals animate loading handoffs. Directional slides encode navigation history. 2	
3	You have a dev server that serves HTML to a browser. An agent in a
4	headless container can't open a browser window — so "run the app" means
5	launching the dev server, driving a headless Chromium against it, and
6	producing a screenshot that proves the page rendered.

9	
10	## Dev server
11	
12	Find the dev command (`package.json` `scripts.dev`, `Makefile`,
13	README), start it in the background, and wait for it to actually serve:
14	
15	```bash
16	npm run dev &   # or yarn dev, pnpm dev, make serve, ./dev.sh
17	timeout 30 bash -c 'until curl -sf http://localhost:3000 >/dev/null; do sleep 1; done'
18	```
19	
20	Don't `sleep 5` — poll the port. Stop by killing the port's listener
21	— `lsof -ti:3000 -sTCP:LISTEN | xargs -r kill` — before relaunching,
22	or the next run hits `EADDRINUSE`. (`$!` after `npm run dev &` is only
23	the npm wrapper; npm doesn't forward SIGTERM to the server it spawned,
24	so the port kill is what actually frees it.) Avoid `pkill -f` with a
25	broad pattern — it can match the agent's own command line and kill the
26	session.
27

29	
30	`chromium-cli` is a headless-Chromium REPL. Pipe a script to stdin:
31	
32	```bash
33	chromium-cli --session app <<'EOF'
34	nav http://localhost:3000
35	wait-for text=Dashboard
36	screenshot
37	click button:has-text("New item")
38	fill input[name="title"] Smoke test
39	press Enter
40	wait-for text=Smoke test
41	screenshot
42	console --errors
43	EOF
44	```
45	
46	Screenshots land in `chromium_cli/sessions/app/screenshots/` (latest
47	symlinked as `screenshot.png`). That's the whole loop: `nav` →
48	`wait-for` the element you need → act (`click` / `fill` / `type` /
49	`press`) → `screenshot` → `console --errors` to check nothing threw.
50	Full command reference: `chromium-cli` skill, or `help` at the prompt.
51	
52	For iterative debugging, run it under tmux and `send-keys` one command
53	at a time — same commands, same session.

58	import `{ chromium }` instead, launch with

## Summary

Implemented view transitions across the product gallery using React's `<ViewTransition>` component and Next.js 16's native App Router integration (no custom animation library, no config flag needed — it works out of the box on canary React, which I installed since the project's pinned `react@19.1.0`/`react-dom@19.1.0` predates the `ViewTransition` API).

**Changes:**
- `package.json` — bumped `react`/`react-dom` to the canary channel that ships `ViewTransition`/`addTransitionType`.
- `tsconfig.json` — added `react/canary` to `types` so `import { ViewTransition } from 'react'` type-checks.
- `app/ProductGrid.tsx` — wrapped each thumbnail in `<ViewTransition name={...} share="morph">` and tagged the `Link` with `transitionTypes={['nav-forward']}`.
- `app/product/[slug]/page.tsx` — matching `name` on the hero image morphs it from the thumbnail; whole page wrapped in a directional `enter`/`exit` `ViewTransition`; the back link tagged `nav-back`; Suspense fallback/content wrapped with `slide-down`/`slide-up` for the skeleton-to-content reveal.
- `app/page.tsx` — same directional wrapper and Suspense-reveal treatment for the grid.
- `app/globals.css` — morph blur, slide/fade keyframes, `::view-transition { pointer-events: none }` so clicks aren't swallowed mid-transition, and a `prefers-reduced-motion` query that zeroes all view-transition animation durations.

I verified this for real rather than just building it: installed a headless Chromium (had to pull missing shared libs via `dnf`) and drove the running dev server with Playwright, inspecting `document.getAnimations()` mid-navigation. Confirmed live: the shared-element morph animation firing on the named image pair, the directional `slide`/`fade` animation on forward and back navigation, and the `fade`/`slide-y` Suspense skeleton→content reveal — and confirmed that with `reducedMotion: 'reduce'` those same animations collapse to instant with no visible motion.
